cse-2024-2-cs-30.approach: Fill an LL(1) table with the two rules: $A \to \alpha$ goes under every terminal of $\text{FIRST}(\alpha)$, and if $\alpha$ can vanish, under every terminal of $\text{FOLLOW}(A)$. Cells (1), (2) need FIRST of the $S$-alternatives; cells (3), (4) need FOLLOW of the nullable $A$ and $B$.
cse-2024-2-cs-30.given: $S \to AaAb \mid BbBa$, $A \to cS \mid \epsilon$, $B \to dS \mid \epsilon$. Unknown cells: (1) $= M[S,c]$, (2) $= M[S,d]$, (3) $= M[A,b]$, (4) $= M[B,a]$.

steps.title: FIRST of A and B
steps.body: $A \to cS \mid \epsilon$ gives $\text{FIRST}(A) = \{c, \epsilon\}$; likewise $\text{FIRST}(B) = \{d, \epsilon\}$. Both are nullable, so whatever follows them inside a body also contributes to FIRST.

steps.title: Cells (1) and (2): FIRST of the S-alternatives
steps.body:
- $\text{FIRST}(AaAb) = (\text{FIRST}(A) - \{\epsilon\}) \cup \{a\} = \{c, a\}$ (if $A \Rightarrow \epsilon$ the body starts with $a$).
- $\text{FIRST}(BbBa) = (\text{FIRST}(B) - \{\epsilon\}) \cup \{b\} = \{d, b\}$.

So $S \to AaAb$ goes under $a$ (given) **and $c$**: cell (1) $= S \to AaAb$. $S \to BbBa$ goes under $b$ (given) **and $d$**: cell (2) $= S \to BbBa$.

steps.title: Cell (3): FOLLOW(A)
steps.body: $A$ appears only in $S \to AaAb$: the first $A$ is followed by $a$ and the second by $b$. Hence $\text{FOLLOW}(A) = \{a, b\}$, and $A \to \epsilon$ is entered under $a$ (given) **and $b$**: cell (3) $= A \to \epsilon$.

steps.title: Cell (4): FOLLOW(B)
steps.body: $B$ appears only in $S \to BbBa$: the first $B$ is followed by $b$ and the second by $a$. Hence $\text{FOLLOW}(B) = \{b, a\}$, and $B \to \epsilon$ goes under $b$ (given) **and $a$**: cell (4) $= B \to \epsilon$.

steps.title: No conflicts, so the combination is (A)
steps.body: Every cell holds at most one rule: $c \notin \text{FOLLOW}(A)$ and $d \notin \text{FOLLOW}(B)$, and the two $S$-alternatives have disjoint FIRST sets $\{a, c\}$ and $\{b, d\}$. The filled cells are (1) $S \to AaAb$, (2) $S \to BbBa$, (3) $A \to \epsilon$, (4) $B \to \epsilon$ — option (A).

optionAnalysis.reason: $c \in \text{FIRST}(AaAb)$, $d \in \text{FIRST}(BbBa)$, and $b \in \text{FOLLOW}(A)$, $a \in \text{FOLLOW}(B)$ fill all four cells exactly this way.
Swaps (1) and (2): $c$ can only begin a string through $A \to cS$, which belongs to $AaAb$, not $BbBa$.

Gets (1) and (2) right but leaves (3), (4) blank — it forgets that $\epsilon$-rules go under FOLLOW: $b \in \text{FOLLOW}(A)$ (the second $A$ in $AaAb$) and $a \in \text{FOLLOW}(B)$ (the second $B$ in $BbBa$).
Both mistakes: swapped $S$-entries and missing $\epsilon$-entries.

cse-2024-2-cs-30.shortcut: Read the given cells: $A \to \epsilon$ is already under $a$, so the rule sits under FOLLOW$(A)$; $A$ is followed by $a$ **and** $b$ in $AaAb$, so (3) cannot be blank — that kills (C), (D). Then $c$ only begins $A$-strings, so (1) uses $AaAb$ — that kills (B).
pitfalls: Looking only at the first $A$ in $AaAb$ (followed by $a$) and missing the second one (followed by $b$).
Forgetting that a nullable leading $A$ lets $a$ itself start $AaAb$ (that is why $S \to AaAb$ is under $a$).
Putting $\epsilon$-rules under FIRST instead of FOLLOW.
cse-2024-2-cs-30.verification: Parse a string: $ab \in L$ ($S \Rightarrow AaAb \Rightarrow ab$): on lookahead $a$ the table picks $S \to AaAb$, $A \to \epsilon$ on $a$, match $a$, then $A$ on lookahead $b$ uses cell (3) $A \to \epsilon$, match $b$ — accepted, so cell (3) must hold $A \to \epsilon$.

cse-2024-2-cs-31.approach: The start state's $\epsilon$-moves split $M$ into two independent branches (through 2 and through 4). Read off each branch's language, take the union, and compare it with the options using a few distinguishing strings.

steps.title: Start: ε-closure of state 1
steps.body: $\epsilon\text{-closure}(1) = \{1, 2, 4\}$. State 2 is accepting, so $\epsilon \in L(M)$. From here the machine commits to the upper branch (via 2) or the lower branch (via 4); no edge connects 4 or 5 back to 2 or 3.

scene.caption: Before any input: $\{1, 2, 4\}$; 2 accepts, so $\epsilon$ is accepted.

steps.title: Upper branch: (00)* and 0(00)*(11)*
steps.body:
Between 2 and 3 every $0$ toggles the state: after an **even** number of 0s we are in 2 (accept), after an **odd** number in 3, whose $\epsilon$-move reaches 5 (accept). From 5, $1$ goes to 4 and $1$ returns to 5, so 5 accepts after any $(11)^*$.

Upper branch: $(00)^* \;+\; 0(00)^*(11)^*$. (After even 0s we sit in 2, which has no 1-move.)

steps.title: Lower branch: 1(11)*
steps.body: From 4, $1$ reaches 5 (accept), and every further $11$ goes $5 \to 4 \to 5$. Lower branch: $1(11)^*$ — an **odd** number of 1s and no 0s.

steps.title: Eliminate the others with test strings
steps.body:
| String | In $L(M)$? | (A) | (C) | (D) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $0$ | yes ($2 \to 3 \to 5$) | no | no | yes |
| $11$ | no | no | yes | no |
| $\epsilon$ | yes | yes | yes | no |
| $00011$ | yes | no | no | no |

Each of (A), (C), (D) disagrees with $M$ on some string; (B) agrees on all of them.

optionAnalysis.reason: Misses every odd run of 0s (e.g. $0$, accepted via $2 \to 3 \xrightarrow{\epsilon} 5$) and the strings $0(00)^*(11)^+$; it ignores the $\epsilon$-edge $3 \to 5$.
With $(00)^*$ chosen as $\epsilon$ it generates $11$, but $11$ is rejected: the lower branch needs an odd number of 1s and the upper branch needs an odd number of 0s before any 1.
Rejects $\epsilon$ (accepted at state 2) and $00011$; it allows only a single $0$ before the $11$ pairs.

cse-2024-2-cs-31.shortcut: Test three strings: $\epsilon$ (kills D), $0$ (kills A), $11$ (kills C).
pitfalls: Ignoring the $\epsilon$-edge $3 \to 5$, which makes odd numbers of 0s acceptable (and allows $11$ pairs after them).
Thinking the run can go back from 5 to the 0-loop — there is no such edge, so 0s can never follow 1s.
Treating $(1 + (00)^*)$ like $(1 + 0(00)^*)$: the former allows an even 0-run (even empty) before $11$.
cse-2024-2-cs-31.verification: Simulated $00011$: $\{1,2,4\} \xrightarrow{0} \{3,5\} \xrightarrow{0} \{2\} \xrightarrow{0} \{3,5\} \xrightarrow{1} \{4\} \xrightarrow{1} \{5\}$ — accepted, and (B) generates it as $0\cdot(00)\cdot(11)$.

cse-2024-2-cs-32.approach: Use the hint as a loop invariant: `first` is $X[i-1]$, `second` is the other value of the current two-value window, `len1` the run of equal values ending at $i$, `len2` the best window ending at $i$. Then decide what each invariant must become in the two branches with blanks.

steps.title: What the variables mean at the start of iteration i
steps.body: At the top of iteration $i$: `first` $= X[i-1]$ (set by `first = X[i]` at the end of the previous iteration), `len1` = length of the run of copies of $X[i-1]$ ending at $i-1$, `len2` = longest window ending at $i-1$ with at most two values, and `second` = the other value in that window.

steps.title: Branch X[i] == second gives (P) = 1
steps.body:
Here $X[i] \ne X[i-1]$ (otherwise the first branch would have run), but $X[i]$ is the window's other value, so the window simply grows: `len2++`.

The run of **equal** values ending at $i$ is just $X[i]$ itself, because $X[i-1]$ is different. So `len1 = 1`: **(P) = 1**. The two values swap roles: `second = first`.

scene.caption: $i = 2$: $X[2] = 1$ equals second; len2 $= 3$, len1 resets to 1.

steps.title: Branch "new value" gives (Q) = len1 + 1
steps.body: Now $X[i]$ is a third value, so the old window cannot be extended. A window ending at $i$ with at most two values may contain only $X[i]$ and $X[i-1]$, and it can reach back only over the **run** of $X[i-1]$ — whose length is `len1`. Hence `len2 = len1 + 1`: **(Q) = len1+1**. Then `len1 = 1`, `second = first`.

scene.caption: $i = 3$: new value 3; window = run of 1 (len1 $= 1$) + 3, so len2 $= 2$.

steps.title: Trace X = [1, 2, 1, 3, 3, 1]
steps.body: With (P) $= 1$, (Q) $=$ len1$+1$ the table shows the values after each iteration. The answer `maxlen` $= 4$ is the subarray $X[2..5] = 1, 3, 3, 1$ (values $\{1, 3\}$), which is indeed the longest one with at most two distinct values.

optionAnalysis.reason: (P) $=$ len1$+1$ treats $X[i]$ as continuing the run of $X[i-1]$, though they differ (on $[1,2,1]$ it makes len1 $= 2$ at $i = 2$); (Q) $=$ len2$+1$ keeps a window with three values.
Both blanks restore the invariants: a value different from $X[i-1]$ starts a new run (len1 $= 1$), and a third value keeps only the run of $X[i-1]$ (len2 $=$ len1 $+ 1$).
(P) is right, but (Q) $=$ len2$+1$ extends the old two-value window by a third value: on $X = [1, 2, 3]$ it returns 3 instead of 2.
(P) $=$ len2$+1$ makes len1 count a mixed window, breaking the "all equal values" meaning; (Q) is right but (P) then corrupts later new-value steps.

cse-2024-2-cs-32.shortcut: Test on $X = [1, 2, 3]$ (answer 2): the third element must give len2 $=$ len1 $+ 1 = 2$, which rules out (A) and (C); and $X = [1, 2, 1, 3]$ needs len1 $= 1$ after the second 1, which rules out (D).
pitfalls: Confusing `len1` (run of one value) with `len2` (window of two values) when a third value arrives.
Forgetting that the branch `X[i] == second` already implies `X[i] != X[i-1]`.
cse-2024-2-cs-32.verification: Brute force on $[1, 2, 1, 3, 3, 1]$: windows with $\le 2$ values have maximum length 4 ($1, 3, 3, 1$), the same as the trace's `maxlen`.

cse-2024-2-cs-33.approach: Triples refer to earlier results by position, so translate the expression bottom-up in evaluation order. An array read needs its own `=[]` triple and an array write needs a `[]=` triple that computes the location, followed by `=` that stores the value.

steps.title: Evaluation order of the right side
steps.body: $(p + r) * -s[i] + u/w$ parses as $\big((p + r) * (-(s[i]))\big) + (u / w)$: unary minus binds tightest, then $*$ and $/$, then $+$.

steps.title: (1): read s[i]
steps.body: Triple (2) is `uminus (1)`, so (1) must be the value $s[i]$. Reading an array element is the indexed-copy triple `=[] s i` (meaning $t = s[i]$). The form `[]=` is the indexed **store** and cannot appear on the right side.

steps.title: (3): multiply (0) by (2)
steps.body: (0) is $p + r$ and (2) is $-s[i]$; the expression multiplies them, so (3) $=$ `* (0) (2)`. Triple (5) `+ (3) (4)` then adds $u/w$ from (4), consistent with this.

steps.title: (6) and (7): store into x[i]
steps.body: Assignment to an array element takes two triples: (6) `[]= x i` names the location $x[i]$, and (7) `= (6) (5)` stores the value of (5) there. So (6) must use the index $i$, not (5).

optionAnalysis.reason: Array read for $s[i]$, product of (0) and (2), array-store location $x[i]$ for (7) — all three match the expression.
`[]=` is a store, not a read of $s[i]$; the operator in (3) is multiplication (the minus is already (2)); and (6) indexes $x$ by (5) instead of $i$.
(1) and (3) are right, but (6) `[]= x (5)` would address $x[\text{value}]$ — the index of $x$ is $i$, and the value (5) is stored by (7).
Wrong read/store operators in (1) and (6) and subtraction instead of multiplication in (3).

cse-2024-2-cs-33.shortcut: (3) must be `*` (the expression has no binary minus) — that leaves (A) and (C); the index of $x$ is $i$, so (A).
pitfalls: Mixing up `=[]` (read: $t = y[i]$) and `[]=` (write: $x[i] = \dots$).
Reading the "$-$" in $* -s[i]$ as a binary subtraction; it is unary minus, already triple (2).
cse-2024-2-cs-33.verification: Re-evaluate the completed list: (0) $p+r$, (1) $s[i]$, (2) $-s[i]$, (3) $(p+r)\cdot(-s[i])$, (4) $u/w$, (5) $(3)+(4)$, (6)–(7) store (5) in $x[i]$ — exactly $x[i] = (p+r) * -s[i] + u/w$.

cse-2024-2-cs-34.approach: Compare pointwise and take expectations: because $0 \le y \le 1$ and $x \ge 0$, every outcome has $xy \le x$, and expectation preserves $\le$. The other options depend on the covariance, which can have either sign — two small examples kill them.

steps.title: Pointwise inequality
steps.body: For every outcome, $x \ge 0$ and $y \le 1$, so $z = xy \le x \cdot 1 = x$. Taking expectations (monotonicity): $\bar{z} = E[xy] \le E[x] = \bar{x}$. Option (D) is always true.

steps.title: Why the other options can fail
steps.body: $\bar{z} = E[xy] = \bar{x}\,\bar{y} + \text{Cov}(x, y)$, and the covariance can be positive, zero or negative.

steps.title: Example 1: positive correlation
steps.body: Let $x = y$ take $0$ or $1$ with probability $\tfrac12$ each. Then $z = x^2 = x$, so $\bar{z} = \tfrac12$, while $\bar{x}\,\bar{y} = \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac14$. Here $\bar{z} > \bar{x}\,\bar{y}$: (A) and (B) fail.

steps.title: Example 2: negative correlation
steps.body: Let $x$ take $0$ or $1$ with probability $\tfrac12$ each and $y = 1 - x$. Then $z = x(1-x) = 0$ always, so $\bar{z} = 0$, while $\bar{x}\,\bar{y} = \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac14$. Here $\bar{z} < \bar{x}\,\bar{y}$: (C) fails. In both examples $\bar{z} \le \bar{x}$ ($\tfrac12 \le \tfrac12$, $0 \le \tfrac12$).

optionAnalysis.reason: Holds only when $\text{Cov}(x,y) = 0$ (e.g. independence); with $x = y \in \{0,1\}$ equally likely, $\bar{z} = \tfrac12 \ne \tfrac14$.
Fails for positively correlated variables: $x = y$ gives $\bar{z} = \tfrac12 > \tfrac14 = \bar{x}\,\bar{y}$.
Fails for negatively correlated variables: $y = 1 - x$ gives $\bar{z} = 0 < \tfrac14$.
$xy \le x$ for every outcome because $0 \le y \le 1$ and $x \ge 0$; expectation keeps the inequality.

cse-2024-2-cs-34.shortcut: "Not necessarily independent" signals that (A)–(C), which are statements about covariance, are traps; only the pointwise bound $xy \le x$ survives.
pitfalls: Assuming $E[xy] = E[x]E[y]$ without independence.
Forgetting that $y \le 1$ is what makes $xy \le x$ (it would fail for $y > 1$).
cse-2024-2-cs-34.verification: By symmetry the same argument gives $\bar{z} \le \bar{y}$, so $\bar{z} \le \min(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$; both examples respect this bound.

cse-2024-2-cs-35.approach: "At least 3 persons" means three different `pid`s in one city, so a query must look at three `Person` tuples together — that needs three copies of the relation, i.e. two cross products. One cross product can see at most two tuples at a time, which is provably not enough.

steps.title: A query with 2 cross products
steps.body:
Rename three copies $P_1, P_2, P_3$ of Person and combine them:
$$\pi_{P_1.city}\Big(\sigma_{\theta}\big(\rho_{P_1}(Person) \times \rho_{P_2}(Person) \times \rho_{P_3}(Person)\big)\Big)$$
Here $\theta$ is $P_1.city = P_2.city \wedge P_2.city = P_3.city \wedge P_1.pid \ne P_2.pid \wedge P_1.pid \ne P_3.pid \wedge P_2.pid \ne P_3.pid$.

A city survives exactly when it has three residents with distinct pids. This uses **2** cross products.

steps.title: Why 1 cross product is not enough
steps.body:
With selection, projection, rename and one cross product, every output tuple is built from **at most two** Person tuples, and these operators are monotone (adding tuples never removes answers).

Suppose such a query $E$ were correct. On a database where city $c$ has three residents, $c$ is output, witnessed by at most two tuples $t_1, t_2$. On the smaller database $\{t_1, t_2\}$ the same tuples still produce $c$, but now $c$ has at most 2 residents — a wrong answer. So one cross product cannot work.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: The minimum number of cross products is **2** (zero products sees one tuple at a time, which cannot even detect two residents).

optionAnalysis.reason: One product pairs two tuples, which detects "at least 2 persons" but cannot distinguish 2 residents from 3.
Three renamed copies of Person need exactly two cross products, and fewer provably cannot work.
Three products would join four copies — enough for "at least 4", more than needed.
Four products are never needed here; the minimum is 2.

cse-2024-2-cs-35.shortcut: "At least $k$" with only $\sigma, \pi, \times, \rho$ needs $k$ copies of the relation, i.e. $k - 1$ cross products; here $k = 3$.
pitfalls: Forgetting the pairwise $pid$ inequalities — without them one person can be matched with himself and every city qualifies.
Counting the copies (3) instead of the products (2).
cse-2024-2-cs-35.verification: Small instance: Person = $\{(1, X), (2, X), (3, X), (4, Y), (5, Y)\}$. The 2-product query outputs only $X$; the best 1-product query (pairs with distinct pids) outputs $X$ and $Y$ — wrong for $Y$.

cse-2024-2-cs-36.approach: `s1` is a mutex, so one thread runs its whole block first. Trace both orders: what matters is that `s2` starts at 0 and only T2 signals it, while T1 waits on it **while still holding** `s1`.

steps.title: T1 gets s1 first
steps.body: T1: `wait(s1)` ($s1: 1 \to 0$), $x = 1$, prints **1**. Then `wait(s2)` with $s2 = 0$ blocks T1 — still holding `s1`. T2's `wait(s1)` blocks too ($s1 = 0$). Only T2 could signal `s2`, and T2 can never get past `wait(s1)`: **deadlock**, T2 prints nothing. This is outcome (C), and it rules out (A).

scene.caption: T1 holds s1 and waits for s2; T2 waits for s1: deadlock.

steps.title: T2 gets s1 first
steps.body: T2: `wait(s1)` ($s1 = 0$), $x = 1$, prints **1**, `signal(s2)` ($s2 = 1$), `signal(s1)` ($s1 = 1$) and finishes. T1 then gets `s1`, $x = 2$, prints **2**, `wait(s2)` succeeds ($s2: 1 \to 0$), `signal(s1)`. Both finish: outcome (B), and (D) is impossible.

scene.caption: T2 first: prints 1, then T1 prints 2, no deadlock.

steps.title: Only these two orders exist
steps.body: Both threads begin with `wait(s1)` and $s1 = 1$, so exactly one enters first and the other blocks until `s1` is signalled. Hence the possible outcomes are exactly (B) and (C).

optionAnalysis.reason: If T1 runs first it blocks on `wait(s2)` while holding `s1`; T2 can never enter to print 2.
T2 never waits on `s2`, so it finishes and signals `s2`; T1 then prints 2 and passes `wait(s2)`.
T1 prints 1, then waits for `s2` (= 0) while holding `s1`; T2 is stuck at `wait(s1)` — a deadlock.
T2 releases `s1` and signals `s2` before finishing, so nothing can block T1 afterwards.

cse-2024-2-cs-36.shortcut: T1 is the only thread that waits on `s2` and it does so inside the critical section, so "T1 first" ⇒ deadlock and "T2 first" ⇒ both print.
pitfalls: Assuming `wait(s2)` in T1 releases `s1` — semaphores do not release each other.
Missing that the deadlock happens **after** T1 prints 1, so (C) says "prints 1" correctly.
cse-2024-2-cs-36.verification: Hold-and-wait check: in (C) T1 holds `s1` and waits for `s2`, T2 holds nothing but waits for `s1`, and `s2` can be raised only by T2 — a circular dependency, so the deadlock is permanent.

cse-2024-2-cs-37.approach: A row swap is left-multiplication by an elementary permutation matrix $E$ with $\det E = -1$. That settles determinant and invertibility at once; symmetry and trace are not preserved, which one 2×2 counterexample each shows.

steps.title: Determinant changes sign
steps.body: $B = EA$ where $E$ is the identity with two rows swapped, $\det E = -1$. So $\det B = \det E \cdot \det A = -\det A$. (A) is TRUE.

steps.title: Invertibility is preserved
steps.body: If $A$ is invertible, $\det A \ne 0$, so $\det B = -\det A \ne 0$ and $B$ is invertible (indeed $B^{-1} = A^{-1}E^{-1}$). (B) is TRUE.

steps.title: Symmetry is lost
steps.body: $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ is symmetric; swapping its rows gives $B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ with $b_{12} = 3 \ne 1 = b_{21}$. (C) is FALSE.

steps.title: Trace is not preserved
steps.body: $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ has trace $0 + 0 = 0$; swapping rows gives $B = I$, with trace $1 + 1 = 2 \ne 0$. (D) is FALSE.

optionAnalysis.reason: $B = EA$ with $\det E = -1$, so $\det B = -\det A$.
$\det B = -\det A \ne 0$ whenever $A$ is invertible.
Counterexample: swapping the rows of $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ gives a non-symmetric matrix. (Symmetry would need the matching columns swapped too.)
Counterexample: $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ (trace 0) becomes $I$ (trace 2); the diagonal entries change.

cse-2024-2-cs-37.shortcut: A row swap is $EA$ with $\det E = -1$, not a similarity $EAE^{-1}$: anything determined by the determinant (A, B) survives, while entry-pattern properties such as symmetry and the diagonal (trace) need not — one 2×2 example each confirms it.
pitfalls: Thinking a row swap is a similarity transform — it is $EA$, not $EAE^{-1}$, so trace and eigenvalues need not survive.
Testing (C) only on the identity, whose swap happens to be symmetric.
cse-2024-2-cs-37.verification: Check (A) on the trace example: $\det\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = -1$ and $\det I = 1 = -(-1)$.

cse-2024-2-cs-38.approach: Simulate each sequence greedily: to output value $v$, it must be on top of S1 (bring it back from S2 with PushToS1, or uncover it by moving the elements above it to S2). A sequence is impossible exactly when uncovering would need more than 2 slots in S2 or when $v$ is buried under something in S2.

steps.title: (A) 100 first is impossible
steps.body: To output 100 first, 400, 300 and 200 must all leave S1 before any output. The only place they can go is S2, which holds just 2 elements. After PushToS2 twice (S2 = 400, 300) the next PushToS2 is not allowed, and 200 still covers 100. (A) cannot be generated.

scene.caption: S2 is full; 200 still covers 100: (A) fails.

steps.title: (B) 200, 300, 400, 100
steps.body: PushToS2, PushToS2 (S2: 400, 300 top), GenerateOutput → **200**; PushToS1, GenerateOutput → **300**; PushToS1, GenerateOutput → **400**; GenerateOutput → **100**. Possible.

scene.caption: After moving 400, 300 to S2 and outputting 200.

steps.title: (C) 400, 200, 100, 300
steps.body: GenerateOutput → **400**; PushToS2 (300 to S2); GenerateOutput → **200**; GenerateOutput → **100**; PushToS1, GenerateOutput → **300**. Possible.

scene.caption: 300 parked in S2 while 200 and 100 are output.

steps.title: (D) 300, 200, 400, 100
steps.body: PushToS2 (400 to S2); GenerateOutput → **300**; GenerateOutput → **200**; PushToS1, GenerateOutput → **400**; GenerateOutput → **100**. Possible.

optionAnalysis.reason: 100 is at the bottom under three elements, but S2 can park only two, so 100 can never be on top while 400, 300, 200 are all unoutput.
Park 400, 300 in S2; output 200; bring back and output 300, then 400; output 100.
Output 400; park 300; output 200 and 100; bring back and output 300.
Park 400; output 300 and 200; bring back and output 400; output 100.

cse-2024-2-cs-38.shortcut: With only 2 parking slots, the first output must be one of the top three (400, 300, 200); that rules out (A) immediately, and the others each need at most 2 parked elements.
pitfalls: Forgetting that S2 is also a stack: an element parked first comes back last.
Ignoring the capacity of S2 (with unlimited S2, 100 could come first).
cse-2024-2-cs-38.verification: In every successful plan S2 never holds more than 2 elements and each PushToS1 returns the element that is needed next, so all moves are legal.

steps.body: Options (A), (B) and (D) all equal $64 = 224_5$; option (C) is $80$, so it is not equal.

optionAnalysis.reason: $224_5 = 64$ in decimal.
$50_{16} = 5 \times 16 = 80 \ne 64$ (the hex value equal to 64 is $40_{16}$).

cse-2024-2-cs-39.shortcut: $64 = 2^6 = 8^2 = 4 \cdot 16$, so in base 8 it is $100$ and in base 16 it is $40$, not $50$.
pitfalls: Reading $224_5$ with weights $10^k$ or mixing up $5^2 = 25$ with $5 \times 2$.
cse-2024-2-cs-39.verification: Back-convert 64 to base 5: $64 = 2 \cdot 25 + 14$, $14 = 2 \cdot 5 + 4$ → digits $2, 2, 4$ ✓; and to base 7: $64 = 1 \cdot 49 + 15$, $15 = 2 \cdot 7 + 1$ → $121$ ✓.

cse-2024-2-cs-40.approach: Work with minterm sets: AND is intersection, OR is union, XOR is symmetric difference. Then convert the final set to both $\sum$ and $\prod$ forms to judge all four options.

steps.title: XOR gate: symmetric difference
steps.body:
$Y = 1$ where exactly one input is 1. Minterms 11 and 13 are in **both** sets, so $Y = 0$ there; the remaining ones are $\{3,5,7\} \cup \{0,1,2,4,6\}$:
$$Y = \textstyle\sum(0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7)$$

steps.title: Express as a product of maxterms
steps.body: The 0s of $Y$ are minterms $8$ to $15$, so $Y = \prod(8,9,10,11,12,13,14,15)$ (in fact $Y = \overline{A}$, the complement of the most significant variable). Options (C) and (D) are both correct.

optionAnalysis.reason: Contains 11 and 13, where both XOR inputs are 1 (so $Y = 0$), and misses 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, where exactly one input is 1.
Its 1s are the minterms not listed, $\{0,1,2,11,13\}$ — the same wrong function as (A).
The symmetric difference of $\{3,5,7,11,13\}$ and $\{0,1,2,4,6,11,13\}$ is exactly $\{0,\dots,7\}$.
$Y$ is 0 exactly on minterms 8–15, so its maxterm list is $(8,\dots,15)$ — the same function as (C).

cse-2024-2-cs-40.shortcut: Only 11 and 13 are common to both gate outputs, so XOR removes them and keeps everything else in the union of the two sets: $\{3,5,7\} \cup \{0,1,2,4,6\}$.
pitfalls: Treating XOR as OR and keeping 11 and 13.
Forgetting that a $\Pi$ list names the 0s, so (C) and (D) describe the same function.

cse-2024-2-cs-41.approach: Use the edge-exchange property of spanning trees: if a cycle had an even edge $e$ and an odd edge $f$, there is a spanning tree $T$ containing $e$ but not $f$, and $T - e + f$ is another spanning tree whose weight differs by an odd amount. So every cycle is parity-uniform; small examples refute the stronger claims.

steps.title: Key fact: swapping two edges of a cycle
steps.body:
Let $C$ be a cycle with edges $e$ and $f$. $C - f$ is a path, so it can be extended to a spanning tree $T$ ($G$ is connected; keep adding edges that do not close a cycle). $f \notin T$, and $T + f$ contains exactly one cycle, namely $C$. Removing $e \in C$ breaks it, so $T' = T - e + f$ is also a spanning tree, and
$$w(T') = w(T) - w(e) + w(f).$$

steps.title: Mixed parities give an odd tree
steps.body:
If $w(e)$ and $w(f)$ have different parities, $w(f) - w(e)$ is odd, so $w(T)$ and $w(T')$ have different parities — one of them is odd, contradicting the hypothesis. Hence in **every cycle all edge weights have the same parity**: (D) is TRUE.

In the picture: swapping $e = RP$ (5) for $f = QR$ (2) turns weight $8$ into $8 - 5 + 2 = 5$, odd.

scene.caption: $T' = \{PQ, QR\}$: weight $3 + 2 = 5$ (odd) — so mixed cycles are impossible.

steps.title: All-odd triangle refutes (A) and (C)
steps.body: Triangle with weights $1, 1, 1$: every spanning tree has 2 edges, weight $1 + 1 = 2$, even. Yet no edge is even, so (A) is FALSE, and the cycle's edges are not all even, so (C) is FALSE.

scene.title: Counterexamples
scene.caption: Every spanning tree weighs 2, but all edges are odd.

steps.title: A tree with mixed weights refutes (B)
steps.body: Let $G$ be the path $P - Q - R - S$ with weights $1, 1, 2$. $G$ is itself its only spanning tree, of weight $1 + 1 + 2 = 4$, even. But its edges are neither all even nor all odd, so (B) is FALSE. (Here (D) holds vacuously — there is no cycle.)

scene.title: Counterexamples
scene.caption: Only spanning tree: weight 4, mixed parities.

answer.value: Only **(D)**: every cycle is all-even or all-odd

optionAnalysis.reason: A triangle with weights $1, 1, 1$ has all spanning trees of weight 2 (even) but only odd edges.
A path with weights $1, 1, 2$ is its own only spanning tree (weight 4) yet mixes parities; edges outside cycles are unconstrained.
The all-odd triangle again: its cycle has only odd edges.
If a cycle had an even and an odd edge, exchanging them in a suitable spanning tree would change the tree's parity, producing an odd spanning tree.

cse-2024-2-cs-41.shortcut: Test the extreme graphs: an odd triangle (spanning trees use 2 odd edges) kills (A) and (C); a tree with mixed weights kills (B).
pitfalls: Assuming the condition forces all edges to share one parity — edges not on any common cycle (bridges) can differ.
Forgetting that an even number of odd edges sums to an even number.
cse-2024-2-cs-41.verification: In the odd triangle all three spanning trees weigh $1+1 = 2$; in the triangle $3, 2, 5$ the trees weigh $5$, $8$, $7$ — two are odd, consistent with the mixed cycle being forbidden.

cse-2024-2-cs-42.approach: Count how often each rule is used in a derivation: with $p$ uses of $S \to aS$, $q$ of $S \to aSbS$ and $r$ of $S \to c$, we get $n_a = p + q$, $n_b = q$, $n_c = r$, and tracking the number of $S$'s gives $r = q + 1$. Every option is then a one-line check.

steps.title: Letters in terms of rule counts
steps.body:
Let a derivation of $w$ use $S \to aS$ $p$ times, $S \to aSbS$ $q$ times and $S \to c$ $r$ times. Each $a$, $b$, $c$ is produced by exactly one rule application:
$$n_a(w) = p + q, \quad n_b(w) = q, \quad n_c(w) = r.$$

steps.title: Count the S symbols
steps.body:
Start with one $S$. $S \to aS$ keeps the number of $S$'s, $S \to aSbS$ increases it by 1, $S \to c$ decreases it by 1. A terminal string has no $S$ left:
$$1 + q - r = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; r = q + 1 \;\Rightarrow\; n_c(w) = n_b(w) + 1.$$
So (C) is TRUE.

steps.title: Check (A) and (B)
steps.body:
$n_a = p + q \ge q = n_b$, with equality when $p = 0$. For $w = c$: $n_a = 0 = n_b$, so $n_a > n_b$ fails: (A) is FALSE.

(B): $n_c - 2 = (n_b + 1) - 2 = n_b - 1 < n_b \le n_a$, so $n_a > n_c - 2$ always: (B) is TRUE.

steps.title: Check (D)
steps.body: $n_c = 2n_b$ means $q + 1 = 2q$, i.e. $q = 1$ only. For $w = c$: $n_c = 1 \ne 0 = 2 n_b$. (D) is FALSE.

optionAnalysis.reason: $n_a \ge n_b$ always, but equality is possible: $w = c$ ($0 = 0$) or $w = acbc$ ($1 = 1$).
$n_c - 2 = n_b - 1 < n_b \le n_a$ for every $w$.
Every $aSbS$ adds one $b$ and one extra $S$, and every $S$ ends as one $c$, so $n_c = n_b + 1$.
Holds only when $n_b = 1$; $w = c$ gives $1 \ne 0$.

cse-2024-2-cs-42.shortcut: Try the shortest words $c$ and $acbc$: both have $n_c = n_b + 1$ and $n_a = n_b$, which kills (A) and (D) at once; (C) is the S-count invariant and (B) follows from it.
pitfalls: Assuming every word has an $a$ — $w = c$ uses no $a$-rule.
Reading (B) as $n_a > n_c$; the "$-2$" makes it always true.
cse-2024-2-cs-42.verification: For $w = aacbc$ (tree shown): $n_a = 2$, $n_b = 1$, $n_c = 2$. (B) $2 > 0$ ✓, (C) $2 = 1 + 1$ ✓, (A) $2 > 1$ holds here but fails for $c$, (D) $2 = 2$ holds here but fails for $c$.
